chapter_text:
CHAPTER 10 — प्रहेलिका (PRAHELIKA)

Introduction — प्रहेलिका किम्?

The word प्रहेलिका (prahelika) means a riddle, a word-puzzle or an enigma. It is formed from the root हेल् / हिल् (to play, to sport) with the prefix प्र, and it names a playful literary form in which a truth or an object is hidden behind a puzzling, seemingly contradictory description. To read a प्रहेलिका you must look past the surface words and discover the one answer (उत्तरम्) that makes every line fit. Sanskrit poets loved this game of hide-and-seek with words; collections such as the प्रहेलिका sections of the काव्य anthologies, the कथासरित्सागर and countless folk manuscripts preserve hundreds of them. In this lesson (NIOS Secondary Sanskrit, Course 209) we read four famous public-domain प्रहेलिकाः, learn their शब्दार्थ (word meanings), translate them into simple English, find the ANSWER of each, and study the wordplay — श्लेष (pun), गूढ (hidden description) and अन्तरालापिका (answer packed into the verse) — that makes a riddle work. Along the way we pick up vocabulary and a little grammar (व्याकरणम्) drawn from the riddles themselves.

Why प्रहेलिका matters (प्रहेलिकायाः महत्त्वम्)

A प्रहेलिका is far more than amusement. First, it sharpens the intellect (बुद्धिः): solving one forces you to weigh every word, notice double meanings, and reason from clues to a conclusion. Second, it builds vocabulary and grammar painlessly — to crack a riddle you must know synonyms (पर्यायाः), case-endings (विभक्तिः), compounds (समासः) and sandhi (सन्धिः). Third, riddles were a favourite entertainment of learned assemblies (विदग्ध-गोष्ठी) and of families on festival nights; asking and answering them was a test of wit and learning. The tradition places प्रहेलिका among the कवि-कौशल (poetic skills): a poet who could compose a clever riddle, or answer one instantly, was admired. Because a good riddle is short, surprising and memorable, it teaches the Sanskrit learner to enjoy the language while thinking hard.

Types of प्रहेलिका (प्रहेलिकानां प्रकाराः)

Traditional rhetoric recognises several kinds. In this lesson three matter most. (1) गूढ / वर्णन-प्रहेलिका — a "hidden-description" riddle: an object is described through a string of apparent contradictions ("lives on a treetop yet is no bird; has three eyes yet is not Shiva"), and the solver must name the single object that satisfies them all. (2) अन्तरालापिका — a riddle whose ANSWER is literally hidden inside the verse itself, most often packed into the last quarter (पाद), so that the words which look like a strange statement are really the replies to the questions asked earlier. (3) श्लेष-प्रहेलिका — a pun-riddle that turns on a word with two meanings (श्लेष = "adhesion"; one sound, two senses). Many riddles mix these devices.

The four riddles (शब्दार्थ सहित)

1) कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात् को हन्ति करिणां कुलम् ।
   किं कुर्यात् कातरो युद्धे मृगात्सिंहः पलायते ॥
   शब्दार्थ: कस्तूरी = musk; जायते = is produced, is born; कस्मात् = from what? (पञ्चमी of किम्); हन्ति = kills; करिणाम् = of elephants (षष्ठी बहुवचन); कुलम् = herd, family; किम् = what; कुर्यात् = would/should do; कातरः = a coward; युद्धे = in battle (सप्तमी); मृगात् = from the deer (पञ्चमी); सिंहः = the lion; पलायते = flees, runs away.
   Type: अन्तरालापिका (प्रश्नोत्तर). The first three quarters ask three questions; the fourth quarter supplies all three answers in order.
   Questions & Answers: (a) From what is musk produced? — मृगात् (from the musk-deer). (b) Who destroys herds of elephants? — सिंहः (the lion). (c) What does a coward do in battle? — पलायते (he flees). Read on its own, the last quarter "मृगात् सिंहः पलायते" seems to say the absurd "a lion flees from a deer," and THAT surface-absurdity is the joke; its real function is to hold the three answers.
   Wordplay: the delight lies in the double reading of the fourth पाद — nonsense on the surface, three neat answers underneath. This is the classic अन्तरालापिका device.

2) भोजनान्ते च किं पेयम् जयन्तः कस्य वै सुतः ।
   कथं विष्णुपदं प्रोक्तं तक्रं शक्रस्य दुर्लभम् ॥
   शब्दार्थ: भोजनान्ते = at the end of a meal (भोजन + अन्ते, सप्तमी); पेयम् = (something) to be drunk; जयन्तः = Jayanta (a proper name); कस्य = whose? (षष्ठी); वै = indeed; सुतः = son; कथम् = how?; विष्णुपदम् = "Vishnu's abode," the supreme state; प्रोक्तम् = said, described; तक्रम् = buttermilk; शक्रस्य = of Indra (शक्र = Indra); दुर्लभम् = hard to obtain.
   Type: अन्तरालापिका (प्रश्नोत्तर). Again three questions, and the last quarter answers all three.
   Questions & Answers: (a) What should be drunk at the end of a meal? — तक्रम् (buttermilk). (b) Whose son is Jayanta? — शक्रस्य (Indra's; Jayanta is the son of Indra). (c) How is the supreme state (विष्णुपद) said to be? — दुर्लभम् (hard to attain). Read together, "तक्रं शक्रस्य दुर्लभम्" playfully reads "buttermilk is hard even for Indra to get," a witty half-truth that conceals the three replies.
   Wordplay: the humour is that the same three words serve two purposes — a stand-alone quip AND the ordered answer-key.

3) वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः त्रिनेत्रधारी न च शूलपाणिः ।
   त्वग्वस्त्रधारी न च सिद्धयोगी जलं च बिभ्रन्न घटो न मेघः ॥
   उत्तरम् (Answer): नारिकेलम् — the coconut (coconut fruit).
   शब्दार्थ: वृक्षाग्रवासी = dwelling at the top of a tree (वृक्ष + अग्र + वासिन्); पक्षिराजः = the king of birds (Garuda); त्रिनेत्रधारी = bearing three eyes; शूलपाणिः = "trident-in-hand," i.e. Shiva; त्वक् = bark, skin, fibre; वस्त्रधारी = wearing as a garment; सिद्धयोगी = an accomplished ascetic; जलम् = water; बिभ्रत् = holding, bearing; घटः = a pot; मेघः = a cloud.
   Type: गूढ / वर्णन-प्रहेलिका (hidden-description). Each phrase pairs a true feature of the coconut with a denial of the god or being it might otherwise suggest.
   How it fits the coconut: it lives at the top of a tree — yet it is no bird-king; it has three "eyes" (the three pores of the shell) — yet it is not three-eyed Shiva; it wears a coat of fibre/bark — yet it is no bark-clad yogi; and it carries water inside — yet it is neither a water-pot nor a rain-cloud. Only the नारिकेल satisfies every clue.
   Wordplay: the engine here is repeated विरोधाभास (apparent contradiction) — "X yet not X-god." Solving it needs knowledge of the coconut's real features and of the deities being hinted at.

4) अपदो दूरगामी च साक्षरो न च पण्डितः ।
   अमुखः स्फुटवक्ता च यो जानाति स पण्डितः ॥
   उत्तरम् (Answer): पत्रम् / लेखः — a written letter (a message on paper/leaf).
   शब्दार्थ: अपदः = footless (अ + पद); दूरगामी = far-going; साक्षरः = "with letters" (सा + अक्षर) and also "literate"; न च पण्डितः = yet not a learned scholar; अमुखः = mouthless; स्फुटवक्ता = a clear speaker; यः जानाति = he who knows (the answer); सः पण्डितः = he (alone) is the true scholar.
   Type: गूढ with a श्लेष. The pun is on साक्षरः: literally "having अक्षर (letters written on it)," but it sounds like "literate / learned," which is at once denied by "न च पण्डितः."
   How it fits a letter: a letter has no feet yet travels far; it is covered with letters yet is not itself a scholar; it has no mouth yet speaks clearly (whoever reads it hears the writer's words). The closing line teases: the one who guesses the answer is the real पण्डित.
   Wordplay: श्लेष on साक्षर, plus a chain of विरोधाभास (footless yet far-going, mouthless yet speaking).

व्याकरणम् — Grammar drawn from the riddles (English explanation, Devanagari examples)

(A) श्लेष (Pun) — the soul of many riddles. श्लेष means "adhesion": a single word "sticks together" two meanings. In riddle 4, साक्षरः = सा (with) + अक्षर (letters) — "having letters on it" — while the very same sound means "literate/learned," a sense the poet at once denies. Recognising a श्लेष means asking, "Could this word mean something else?" Wherever a riddle seems self-contradictory, suspect a pun or a hidden second sense.

(B) अन्तरालापिका structure. In riddles 1 and 2 the ANSWER is not outside the verse but inside it — the last quarter (चतुर्थः पादः) is the answer-key. Learn to test the final पाद both ways: as a stand-alone (often absurd or witty) sentence, and as an ordered list of replies to the earlier questions. "मृगात् सिंहः पलायते" and "तक्रं शक्रस्य दुर्लभम्" are the two model examples.

(C) सन्धि (Sandhi). Splitting joined forms (सन्धि-विच्छेद) is the first step in reading a riddle.
  • वृक्ष + अग्र = वृक्षाग्र (अ + अ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि) — "tree-top", in वृक्षाग्रवासी.
  • भोजन + अन्ते = भोजनान्ते (अ + अ = आ) — "at the meal's end."
  • बिभ्रत् + न = बिभ्रन्न (त् before न → न्, व्यञ्जन-सन्धि) — "bearing (water), (it is) not..."
  • न + च = often written together; and सा + अक्षर = साक्षर (आ merges) in riddle 4.
  • मृगात् + सिंहः: the visarga/त् boundary is heard as the answer मृगात् then सिंहः.

(D) विभक्ति (Case endings). The riddles are rich in cases.
  • पञ्चमी (ablative, "from"): कस्मात् "from what", मृगात् "from the deer."
  • षष्ठी (genitive, "of/whose"): करिणाम् "of elephants" (plural), कस्य "whose", शक्रस्य "of Indra."
  • सप्तमी (locative, "in/at"): युद्धे "in battle", भोजनान्ते "at the end of the meal."
  • प्रथमा (nominative, subject): सिंहः "the lion", घटः "a pot", मेघः "a cloud", पण्डितः "the scholar."
  • द्वितीया (accusative, object): कुलम् "the herd", जलम् "water", विष्णुपदम् "the supreme state."

(E) समास (Compounds). Riddles love compounds because they pack description tightly.
  • वृक्षाग्रवासी = वृक्षस्य अग्रे वासी ("dweller at the tree-top") — an उपपद-तत्पुरुष.
  • पक्षिराजः = पक्षिणां राजा ("king of birds") — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष.
  • शूलपाणिः = शूलं पाणौ यस्य सः ("he in whose hand is a trident," = Shiva) — बहुव्रीहि.
  • त्रिनेत्रधारी = त्रीणि नेत्राणि धारयति ("bearing three eyes"); त्वग्वस्त्रधारी = "wearing bark as a garment."
  • भोजनान्ते = भोजनस्य अन्ते ("at the end of the meal") — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष.
Splitting such compounds (समास-विग्रह) unlocks the clue behind each phrase.

SUMMARY (सारांश)

In this chapter you learned that a प्रहेलिका is a Sanskrit riddle — a playful verse that hides an answer behind a puzzling, often self-contradictory description. You met three devices: गूढ / वर्णन (hidden description), अन्तरालापिका (answer packed into the verse, usually the last quarter) and श्लेष (pun). You read four famous public-domain riddles: the प्रश्नोत्तर pair "कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात्..." (answers मृगात् / सिंहः / पलायते) and "भोजनान्ते च किं पेयम्..." (answers तक्रम् / शक्रस्य / दुर्लभम्); the coconut riddle "वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः..." (उत्तरम् नारिकेलम्); and the letter riddle "अपदो दूरगामी च साक्षरो न च पण्डितः..." (उत्तरम् पत्रम्). For each you studied the शब्दार्थ, an English translation, the ANSWER and the wordplay that makes it work. Finally you drew grammar from the riddles — श्लेष, सन्धि-विच्छेद, the common विभक्ति case-endings and समास-विग्रह of compounds like वृक्षाग्रवासी and शूलपाणिः. Solving riddles is thus a delightful way to sharpen the mind while mastering Sanskrit words and grammar. यो जानाति स पण्डितः — "he who knows (the answer) is the true scholar."

sections.heading: What a प्रहेलिका is and why it matters
bullets: प्रहेलिका = a riddle or word-puzzle (from प्र + हेल्, 'to play'); an answer is hidden behind a puzzling, often self-contradictory description.

sections.heading: The three types of wordplay

sections.heading: The four riddles and their answers
bullets: कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात्...: answers मृगात् (musk from the deer), सिंहः (the lion kills elephants), पलायते (a coward flees).
भोजनान्ते च किं पेयम्...: answers तक्रम् (buttermilk), शक्रस्य (Jayanta is Indra's son), दुर्लभम् (the supreme state is hard to attain).
वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः...: उत्तरम् नारिकेलम् — the coconut (three 'eyes', fibre coat, water inside).
अपदो दूरगामी च साक्षरो न च पण्डितः...: उत्तरम् पत्रम् — a letter (footless yet far-going, mouthless yet speaking).

sections.heading: Sandhi and Samasa from the riddles
bullets: सन्धि-विच्छेद: वृक्षाग्र = वृक्ष + अग्र (अ+अ=आ); भोजनान्ते = भोजन + अन्ते; साक्षर = सा + अक्षर.

वृक्षाग्रवासी = वृक्षस्य अग्रे वासी (उपपद-तत्पुरुष); त्रिनेत्रधारी = त्रीणि नेत्राणि धारयति.
Splitting sandhi and compounds is the first step in reading any riddle.

sections.heading: Vibhakti in the riddles
bullets: पञ्चमी (ablative, 'from'): कस्मात् 'from what', मृगात् 'from the deer'.
षष्ठी (genitive, 'of/whose'): करिणाम् 'of elephants', कस्य 'whose', शक्रस्य 'of Indra'.

key_takeaways: A प्रहेलिका (प्र + हेल्, 'to play') is a Sanskrit riddle: an answer hidden behind a puzzling, often self-contradictory description.
Three devices power riddles — गूढ/वर्णन (hidden description), अन्तरालापिका (answer inside the verse) and श्लेष (pun).
In an अन्तरालापिका the last quarter is the answer-key: 'मृगात् सिंहः पलायते' and 'तक्रं शक्रस्य दुर्लभम्' both hide three replies.
The coconut riddle (वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः) is solved as नारिकेलम्; the letter riddle (अपदो दूरगामी) as पत्रम्.
श्लेष on साक्षरः ('having letters' / 'literate') and chains of विरोधाभास (footless yet far-going) are typical riddle tricks.
सन्धि-विच्छेद (वृक्षाग्र = वृक्ष + अग्र) and समास-विग्रह (पक्षिराजः = पक्षिणां राजा) are the first steps in reading a riddle.
विभक्ति endings show a word's role: पञ्चमी 'from' (मृगात्), षष्ठी 'of' (शक्रस्य), सप्तमी 'in' (युद्धे).

glossary.definition: A riddle, word-puzzle or enigma (from प्र + हेल्, 'to play'); a verse that hides an answer behind a puzzling description.
The answer or solution to a riddle; the single object or word that makes every clue of the प्रहेलिका fit.
A 'hidden-description' riddle in which an object is described by contradictions, e.g. the coconut riddle answered नारिकेलम्.
A riddle whose answer is packed inside the verse itself, usually into the last quarter (पाद).
A pun ('adhesion'): one word carrying two meanings at once, e.g. साक्षरः = 'having letters' and 'literate'.
Apparent contradiction; the riddle-device of 'X yet not X' (footless yet far-going) resolved by the hidden answer.
The coconut — the answer to 'वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः...'; treetop-dweller with three 'eyes', fibre coat and water within.
A written letter/message — the answer to 'अपदो दूरगामी...'; footless yet far-going, mouthless yet speaking.
Musk; in riddle 1 it is 'produced from the deer' (मृगात्), a musk-deer.
Buttermilk; the answer to 'what should be drunk at the end of a meal?' in riddle 2.
A name of Indra; in riddle 2 Jayanta is called शक्रस्य सुतः, 'Indra's son'.
Splitting a joined (sandhi) form back into its words, e.g. वृक्षाग्र = वृक्ष + अग्र; the first step in reading a riddle.
Analysing a compound into its parts, e.g. पक्षिराजः = पक्षिणां राजा ('king of birds').
A noun's case ending, showing its role: पञ्चमी 'from', षष्ठी 'of', सप्तमी 'in', प्रथमा subject, द्वितीया object.
'Trident-in-hand', a name of Shiva (बहुव्रीहि = शूलं पाणौ यस्य); denied of the coconut in riddle 3.

Translate and solve the riddle:

Clues: (i) it grows at the top of the coconut palm, yet is no bird; (ii) it has three 'eyes' (the three pores of the shell), yet is not three-eyed Shiva.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English word meaning) of each: कस्तूरी, करिणाम्, पलायते, तक्रम्, दुर्लभम्.

questions.question: What is a प्रहेलिका? Name the three main types of wordplay used in riddles.
questions.answer: A प्रहेलिका is a Sanskrit riddle or word-puzzle in which an answer is hidden behind a puzzling, often self-contradictory description. The three main types are: गूढ/वर्णन (hidden description), अन्तरालापिका (answer packed inside the verse) and श्लेष (pun).

questions.question: Explain the अन्तरालापिका wordplay in 'कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात्...मृगात्सिंहः पलायते'. Why is the last quarter special?
questions.answer: The first three quarters ask three questions and the fourth quarter answers all three in order: कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात् → मृगात् (from the deer); को हन्ति करिणां कुलम् → सिंहः (the lion); किं कुर्यात् कातरो युद्धे → पलायते (he flees). The last quarter 'मृगात् सिंहः पलायते' read alone seems to say the absurd 'a lion flees from a deer' — that surface-nonsense is the joke, while its real job is to hold the three answers. That double function makes it an अन्तरालापिका.
questions.explanation: Answer hidden in the fourth पाद.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद (split) of: (a) वृक्षाग्र (b) भोजनान्ते.
questions.answer: (a) वृक्षाग्र = वृक्ष + अग्र (अ + अ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि). (b) भोजनान्ते = भोजन + अन्ते (अ + अ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि).
questions.explanation: Splitting joined forms from the riddles.

questions.question: State the विभक्ति (case) and meaning-role of each: मृगात्, करिणाम्, युद्धे.
questions.answer: मृगात् = पञ्चमी (ablative) → 'from the deer'. करिणाम् = षष्ठी (genitive) plural → 'of the elephants'. युद्धे = सप्तमी (locative) → 'in battle'.

questions.question: Take the riddle 'अपदो दूरगामी च साक्षरो न च पण्डितः, अमुखः स्फुटवक्ता च यो जानाति स पण्डितः'. Give its word meanings, the ANSWER, and a full explanation of how each clue fits.
questions.answer: शब्दार्थ: अपदः = footless; दूरगामी = far-going; साक्षरः = 'with letters' (and, punningly, 'literate'); न च पण्डितः = yet not a scholar; अमुखः = mouthless; स्फुटवक्ता = a clear speaker; यः जानाति = he who knows; सः पण्डितः = he is the (true) scholar. ANSWER: पत्रम्/लेखः (a written letter). Explanation: a letter has no feet, yet it travels far (दूरगामी); it is covered with letters (साक्षरः), yet is not itself learned; it has no mouth, yet it speaks clearly, because whoever reads it hears the writer's words. The closing line teasingly says that whoever guesses the answer is the real पण्डित. The wordplay is a श्लेष on साक्षरः plus a chain of विरोधाभास (footless yet far-going, mouthless yet speaking).

questions.answer: A प्रहेलिका is a Sanskrit riddle or word-puzzle in which an answer (an object, word or idea) is hidden behind a puzzling, often self-contradictory description. The solver must find the single answer that makes every clue fit.

questions.question: Name and briefly explain the three main types of प्रहेलिका studied in this lesson.
questions.answer: (1) गूढ / वर्णन — a hidden-description riddle: an object is described by contradictions ('lives on a treetop yet is no bird') and the solver names it. (2) अन्तरालापिका — the answer is packed inside the verse, usually the last quarter, which reads both as a witty line and as the answers. (3) श्लेष — a pun-riddle turning on one word with two meanings.

questions.question: Give the three answers hidden in the last quarter of 'कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात्...'.
questions.answer: मृगात् (musk is produced from the deer), सिंहः (the lion destroys herds of elephants), and पलायते (a coward flees in battle).

questions.question: Write, in Devanagari, the answers to the coconut riddle and the letter riddle.
questions.answer: Coconut riddle 'वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः...' → नारिकेलम्. Letter riddle 'अपदो दूरगामी...' → पत्रम् (लेखः).

questions.question: Explain how the coconut fits the clue 'त्रिनेत्रधारी न च शूलपाणिः'.
questions.answer: त्रिनेत्रधारी means 'three-eyed': the coconut shell has three eye-like pores, so it 'bears three eyes'. But न च शूलपाणिः denies that it is Shiva, who is also three-eyed and holds a trident. So the clue says: it is three-eyed like Shiva, yet it is only a coconut, not the god.
questions.explanation: Three eyes of the coconut vs Shiva.

questions.question: Why is a letter called 'अमुखः स्फुटवक्ता' (mouthless yet a clear speaker)?
questions.answer: A letter has no mouth, yet it 'speaks' clearly: whoever reads it receives the writer's exact words. So though mouthless, it communicates as if speaking.
questions.explanation: A letter speaks through its writing.

questions.question: Explain the surface meaning and the real function of 'तक्रं शक्रस्य दुर्लभम्'.
questions.answer: On the surface it reads 'buttermilk (तक्रम्) is hard to obtain even for Indra (शक्र)' — a witty half-truth. Its real function is to answer the three earlier questions in order: तक्रम् (drink after a meal), शक्रस्य (Jayanta is Indra's son), दुर्लभम् (the supreme state is hard to attain).
questions.explanation: Double reading of the last पाद.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: करिणाम्, कातरः, पलायते.
questions.answer: करिणाम् = of the elephants (genitive plural); कातरः = a coward; पलायते = flees / runs away.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: तक्रम्, शक्रस्य, दुर्लभम्.
questions.answer: तक्रम् = buttermilk; शक्रस्य = of Indra; दुर्लभम् = hard to obtain.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: वृक्षाग्रवासी, त्रिनेत्रधारी, त्वग्वस्त्रधारी.
questions.answer: वृक्षाग्रवासी = dwelling at the top of a tree; त्रिनेत्रधारी = bearing three eyes; त्वग्वस्त्रधारी = wearing bark/fibre as a garment.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: अपदः, दूरगामी, स्फुटवक्ता.
questions.answer: अपदः = footless; दूरगामी = far-going; स्फुटवक्ता = a clear speaker.

questions.question: Analyse the श्लेष (pun) in 'साक्षरो न च पण्डितः'.
questions.answer: साक्षरः has two senses: literally सा + अक्षर = 'having letters (written on it)', which fits a letter; and it sounds like 'literate / learned'. The phrase न च पण्डितः at once denies the second sense — the letter is covered with अक्षर yet is not itself a scholar. The clash of the two meanings is the pun that points to the answer, पत्रम्.

questions.question: What makes a riddle an अन्तरालापिका? Give one example from the lesson.
questions.answer: In an अन्तरालापिका the ANSWER is hidden inside the verse itself, usually in the last quarter, which reads both as a witty statement and as the ordered answers. Example: 'मृगात् सिंहः पलायते' in riddle 1, which answers the three questions मृगात् / सिंहः / पलायते.

questions.question: Explain the विरोधाभास (apparent contradiction) device using the letter riddle.
questions.answer: The letter riddle piles up 'X yet not X' clues: footless (अपदः) yet far-going (दूरगामी); covered with letters yet not learned; mouthless (अमुखः) yet a clear speaker (स्फुटवक्ता). Each seems self-contradictory, but all are resolved by the single answer 'a letter' (पत्रम्).

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of: (a) वृक्षाग्र (b) भोजनान्ते.
questions.answer: (a) वृक्षाग्र = वृक्ष + अग्र (अ + अ = आ). (b) भोजनान्ते = भोजन + अन्ते (अ + अ = आ). Both are दीर्घ-सन्धि.

questions.question: What is दीर्घ-सन्धि? Give one example from the riddles.
questions.answer: दीर्घ-सन्धि is the rule by which a short vowel meeting a similar vowel merges into a single long vowel. Example from the riddles: वृक्ष + अग्र = वृक्षाग्र (अ + अ = आ).

questions.question: Give the विभक्ति (case) and role of: (a) करिणाम् (b) युद्धे.
questions.answer: (a) करिणाम् = षष्ठी (genitive), plural — 'of the elephants'. (b) युद्धे = सप्तमी (locative), singular — 'in battle'.

questions.question: Do the समास-विग्रह of: (a) पक्षिराजः (b) शूलपाणिः.
questions.answer: (a) पक्षिराजः = पक्षिणां राजा ('king of birds'), a षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष. (b) शूलपाणिः = शूलं पाणौ यस्य सः ('he in whose hand is a trident', = Shiva), a बहुव्रीहि.

questions.question: Translate into English: 'को हन्ति करिणां कुलम्'.
questions.answer: 'Who destroys the herd of elephants?' — कः (who) हन्ति (kills) करिणां कुलम् (the herd of elephants). Answer: सिंहः (the lion).

questions.question: Solve the riddle 'अपदो दूरगामी च साक्षरो न च पण्डितः'. Give the answer and two supporting reasons.
questions.answer: Answer: पत्रम् (a written letter). Reasons: (i) अपदः (footless) यत् दूरगामी — a letter has no feet yet is carried far; (ii) साक्षरः न च पण्डितः — it is covered with letters yet is not itself a scholar. (Also amukhaḥ yet clear-speaking.)

questions.question: Translate 'भोजनान्ते च किं पेयम् जयन्तः कस्य वै सुतः' and give the two answers.
questions.answer: 'What should be drunk at the end of a meal? Whose son is Jayanta?' Answers: तक्रम् (buttermilk) and शक्रस्य (Indra's — Jayanta is the son of Indra).

questions.question: Explain why the coconut is called 'जलं च बिभ्रन्न घटो न मेघः'.
questions.answer: It means 'bearing water, yet neither a pot nor a cloud'. A coconut carries water inside it (coconut water), so it 'bears water' like a pot or a rain-cloud — yet it is obviously neither; it is only a coconut. This contradiction is one more clue to the answer नारिकेलम्.

questions.question: What is a प्रहेलिका? Explain its meaning, its value, and the three main types of wordplay used in riddles.
questions.answer:
A प्रहेलिका is a Sanskrit riddle or word-puzzle. The word comes from प्र + हेल् ('to play, to sport'), so it names a playful form in which an answer is hidden behind a puzzling, often self-contradictory description; the solver must find the one answer that makes every clue fit.
Riddles are valued because they sharpen the intellect (every word must be weighed), and because cracking them teaches synonyms, सन्धि, विभक्ति and समास painlessly. They were a favourite of learned assemblies and of families on festival nights, and count among the कवि-कौशल (poetic skills).
Three types of wordplay matter most: (1) गूढ / वर्णन — a hidden-description riddle where an object is shown through contradictions and then named (e.g. the coconut); (2) अन्तरालापिका — a riddle whose answer is packed inside the verse, usually the last quarter, which reads both as a witty statement and as the answers; and (3) श्लेष — a pun-riddle that turns on one word carrying two meanings.

questions.question: Write any TWO riddles from the lesson in Devanagari and give the ANSWER of each.
questions.answer:
1. कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात् को हन्ति करिणां कुलम्। किं कुर्यात् कातरो युद्धे मृगात्सिंहः पलायते॥ — Answers: मृगात् (musk from the deer), सिंहः (the lion kills elephants), पलायते (a coward flees).
2. वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः त्रिनेत्रधारी न च शूलपाणिः। त्वग्वस्त्रधारी न च सिद्धयोगी जलं च बिभ्रन्न घटो न मेघः॥ — उत्तरम्: नारिकेलम् (the coconut).

questions.question: Take the coconut riddle 'वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः...'. Give the word meanings and explain, clue by clue, how each fits the coconut.
questions.answer:
शब्दार्थ: वृक्षाग्रवासी = dwelling at the tree-top; पक्षिराजः = king of birds (Garuda); त्रिनेत्रधारी = three-eyed; शूलपाणिः = trident-holder (Shiva); त्वक् = bark/fibre; वस्त्रधारी = wearing as a garment; सिद्धयोगी = accomplished ascetic; जलम् = water; बिभ्रत् = bearing; घटः = pot; मेघः = cloud. उत्तरम्: नारिकेलम् (the coconut).
Clue by clue: (1) it lives at the top of the coconut palm (वृक्षाग्रवासी) yet is no bird-king; (2) it has three 'eyes' — the three pores of the shell (त्रिनेत्रधारी) — yet is not three-eyed Shiva; (3) it wears a coat of fibre/bark (त्वग्वस्त्रधारी) yet is no bark-clad yogi; (4) it carries water inside (जलं बिभ्रत्) yet is neither a water-pot nor a rain-cloud. Only the coconut satisfies all four contradictions, so the answer is नारिकेलम्.

questions.question: Collect and give the शब्दार्थ of at least EIGHT Sanskrit words drawn from the four riddles.
questions.answer: कस्तूरी = musk; करिणाम् = of elephants; पलायते = flees; तक्रम् = buttermilk; शक्रस्य = of Indra; दुर्लभम् = hard to obtain; वृक्षाग्रवासी = dwelling at a tree-top; पक्षिराजः = king of birds; त्रिनेत्रधारी = three-eyed; शूलपाणिः = Shiva (trident-holder); अपदः = footless; दूरगामी = far-going; साक्षरः = having letters / 'literate'; स्फुटवक्ता = a clear speaker. (Any eight correctly explained are acceptable.)

questions.question: Discuss the wordplay of the riddles, using the अन्तरालापिका of riddle 1 and the श्लेष of the letter riddle as examples.
questions.answer:
Sanskrit riddles delight because of their wordplay. In riddle 1, 'कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात्... मृगात्सिंहः पलायते', the device is अन्तरालापिका: the first three quarters ask three questions and the fourth quarter answers all three in order — मृगात् (from the deer), सिंहः (the lion), पलायते (flees). Read on its own the fourth quarter seems to say the absurd 'a lion flees from a deer'; that surface-nonsense is the joke, while its true job is to hold the answers. So the same words work two ways at once.
In the letter riddle, 'अपदो दूरगामी च साक्षरो न च पण्डितः...', the device is श्लेष (pun) joined with विरोधाभास. साक्षरः means both 'having letters (written on it)' and 'literate/learned'; the phrase न च पण्डितः instantly denies the second sense. Around this pun the poet stacks contradictions — footless yet far-going, mouthless yet clear-speaking — all resolved by one answer, पत्रम् (a letter). Thus riddles reward the reader who notices double meanings and tests every clue against a single solution.

questions.question: Explain सन्धि and सन्धि-विच्छेद with four examples taken from the riddles of this chapter.
questions.answer:
सन्धि is the joining/merging of sounds where two words meet; सन्धि-विच्छेद is splitting such a joined form back into its separate words. Examples from the riddles:
1. वृक्ष + अग्र = वृक्षाग्र (अ + अ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि) — in वृक्षाग्रवासी.
2. भोजन + अन्ते = भोजनान्ते (अ + अ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि).
3. सा + अक्षर = साक्षर (आ absorbs अ) — the pun-word of the letter riddle.
4. बिभ्रत् + न = बिभ्रन्न (त् changes before न, व्यञ्जन-सन्धि) — 'bearing (water), (it is) not...'.
Being able both to join (सन्धि) and to split (सन्धि-विच्छेद) is the first step in reading any riddle correctly.

questions.question: Using words from the riddles, explain the common विभक्ति (cases) and the समास-विग्रह of two compounds.
questions.answer:
विभक्ति (case endings) show a word's role. From the riddles: पञ्चमी (ablative, 'from') — कस्मात् 'from what', मृगात् 'from the deer'; षष्ठी (genitive, 'of') — करिणाम् 'of elephants', शक्रस्य 'of Indra'; सप्तमी (locative, 'in/at') — युद्धे 'in battle', भोजनान्ते 'at the meal's end'; प्रथमा (subject) — सिंहः, घटः, मेघः; द्वितीया (object) — कुलम्, जलम्, विष्णुपदम्.
समास-विग्रह (compound analysis): पक्षिराजः = पक्षिणां राजा ('king of birds', a षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष); शूलपाणिः = शूलं पाणौ यस्य सः ('he in whose hand is a trident', = Shiva, a बहुव्रीहि). Splitting cases and compounds unlocks the meaning of each clue.

questions.question: Translate the riddle 'कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात् को हन्ति करिणां कुलम्, किं कुर्यात् कातरो युद्धे मृगात्सिंहः पलायते' and explain how it is solved.
questions.answer: Translation of the three questions: 'From what is musk produced? Who destroys the herd of elephants? What does a coward do in battle?' The fourth quarter 'मृगात् सिंहः पलायते' answers them in order: मृगात् (musk comes from the deer), सिंहः (the lion destroys elephants), पलायते (a coward flees). It is solved by recognising the अन्तरालापिका structure: instead of reading the last quarter as one sentence (which would absurdly mean 'a lion flees from a deer'), we read it as the three separate answers to the three questions. That double reading is the whole delight of the riddle.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात् को हन्ति करिणां कुलम्।
किं कुर्यात् कातरो युद्धे मृगात्सिंहः पलायते॥
(a) From what is musk produced? (b) Who kills herds of elephants? (c) In which विभक्ति is 'करिणाम्'? (d) What type of riddle is this?
questions.answer: (a) मृगात् — from the (musk) deer. (b) सिंहः — the lion. (c) करिणाम् is षष्ठी (genitive) plural, 'of the elephants'. (d) It is an अन्तरालापिका (प्रश्नोत्तर): the last quarter answers all three questions.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
भोजनान्ते च किं पेयम् जयन्तः कस्य वै सुतः।
कथं विष्णुपदं प्रोक्तं तक्रं शक्रस्य दुर्लभम्॥
(a) What is drunk after a meal? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'सुतः'. (c) Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'भोजनान्ते'. (d) Whose son is Jayanta?
questions.answer: (a) तक्रम् (buttermilk). (b) सुतः = son. (c) भोजनान्ते = भोजन + अन्ते. (d) शक्रस्य — Indra's (Jayanta is Indra's son).
questions.explanation: Comprehension of riddle 2 with a sandhi split.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः त्रिनेत्रधारी न च शूलपाणिः।
त्वग्वस्त्रधारी न च सिद्धयोगी जलं च बिभ्रन्न घटो न मेघः॥
(a) What is the ANSWER? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'पक्षिराजः'. (c) What do the three 'eyes' refer to? (d) What device drives this riddle?
questions.answer: (a) नारिकेलम् (the coconut). (b) पक्षिराजः = king of birds (Garuda). (c) The three 'eyes' are the three pores on the coconut shell. (d) The device is गूढ/वर्णन with repeated विरोधाभास ('X yet not the X-god').

questions.question:
Read and answer:
अपदो दूरगामी च साक्षरो न च पण्डितः।
अमुखः स्फुटवक्ता च यो जानाति स पण्डितः॥
(a) What is the ANSWER? (b) On which word does the श्लेष (pun) turn? (c) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'अमुखः'. (d) Explain the pun in one sentence.
questions.answer: (a) पत्रम् (a written letter). (b) The pun turns on साक्षरः. (c) अमुखः = mouthless. (d) साक्षरः means both 'having letters written on it' (true of a letter) and 'literate/learned', a sense at once denied by न च पण्डितः.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः...
(a) Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'वृक्षाग्र'. (b) Which सन्धि is it? (c) Do the समास-विग्रह of 'वृक्षाग्रवासी'. (d) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'शूलपाणिः'.
questions.answer: (a) वृक्षाग्र = वृक्ष + अग्र. (b) दीर्घ-सन्धि (अ + अ = आ). (c) वृक्षाग्रवासी = वृक्षस्य अग्रे वासी ('dweller at the tree-top'). (d) शूलपाणिः = Shiva, 'the trident-holder'.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात्...
(a) In which विभक्ति is 'कस्मात्'? (b) In which विभक्ति is 'मृगात्'? (c) What do both endings mean in English? (d) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'कातरः'.
questions.answer: (a) कस्मात् is पञ्चमी (ablative) of किम्. (b) मृगात् is पञ्चमी (ablative). (c) The -आत् / ablative ending means 'from'. (d) कातरः = a coward.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
अपदो दूरगामी च साक्षरो न च पण्डितः।
(a) What is the ANSWER? (b) Translate 'अपदो दूरगामी'. (c) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'दूरगामी'. (d) Why is it 'mouthless yet clear-speaking'?
questions.answer: (a) पत्रम् (a letter). (b) 'Footless, yet far-going.' (c) दूरगामी = far-going. (d) A letter has no mouth, yet it 'speaks' clearly because the reader receives the writer's words.

questions.question:
A quiz-master reads four riddles. Match each to its answer:
(i) कस्तूरी जायते कस्मात्... (ii) भोजनान्ते च किं पेयम्... (iii) वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः... (iv) अपदो दूरगामी...
Give the main answer of each.
questions.answer: (i) मृगात् / सिंहः / पलायते (the three packed answers). (ii) तक्रम् / शक्रस्य / दुर्लभम्. (iii) नारिकेलम् (the coconut). (iv) पत्रम् (a letter).

questions.question:
Read and answer:
'तक्रं शक्रस्य दुर्लभम्' (the last quarter of riddle 2).
(a) What does it seem to say on the surface? (b) What three answers does it really give? (c) What type of riddle uses this trick? (d) Why is it witty?
questions.answer: (a) On the surface: 'buttermilk (तक्रम्) is hard to obtain even for Indra (शक्र)'. (b) Really it answers: तक्रम् (drink after a meal), शक्रस्य (Jayanta is Indra's son), दुर्लभम् (the supreme state is hard to attain). (c) An अन्तरालापिका. (d) It is witty because the same three words are both a joke and the exact answer-key.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
वृक्षाग्रवासी न च पक्षिराजः त्रिनेत्रधारी न च शूलपाणिः।
(a) Which two beings are hinted at and denied? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'त्रिनेत्रधारी'. (c) What single object fits both clues? (d) In one line, state how the riddle is built.
questions.answer: (a) Garuda (पक्षिराज, king of birds) and Shiva (शूलपाणि, three-eyed trident-holder). (b) त्रिनेत्रधारी = bearing three eyes. (c) The coconut (नारिकेलम्). (d) It is built by affirming a feature and denying the deity that feature might suggest — 'X yet not the X-god'.
